opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the simplest way to put it is that intelligence, at least the kind we actually care about, has never really been a single-agent phenomenon. If you look at where human intelligence comes from, a huge part of it is social. We evolved in groups, we had to coordinate, compete, communicate, figure out what other people were thinking and what they wanted. Language itself is fundamentally a multi-agent invention. So if we're trying to build systems that are genuinely intelligent, it would be strange to think we can get there by training one agent in isolation against a static environment.

The second reason is more practical. We're now at a point where we're deploying lots of AI systems into the real world, and they're not going to be operating alone. They'll be interacting with humans, with each other, with other companies' models, in markets, in negotiations, on the internet. And the moment you have more than one learning agent in an environment, the problem changes qualitatively. The environment is no longer stationary, because the other agents are adapting too. Things that look optimal from a single-agent perspective can lead to terrible collective outcomes. You get social dilemmas, you get arms races, you get miscoordination. A lot of the classic machine learning toolkit just wasn't designed with that in mind.

And the third thing, which I find really exciting, is that multi-agent settings are also a source of open-endedness. When agents co-adapt, they create curricula for each other. Self-play gave us things like superhuman Go, but that's the tip of the iceberg. If we can understand how to get populations of agents to keep generating new challenges, new skills, new conventions, that might be one of the most scalable paths to more general capabilities, rather than relying on humans to hand-design every task.

So to me it's both a capabilities question and a safety question. We need to understand how to get agents that can cooperate, that can reason about others, that can coordinate with humans they've never met before, and that don't fall into these bad equilibria. That's exactly the set of problems multi-agent learning is about, and I think it's going to become more and more central as these systems get deployed at scale.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that almost everything we care about in intelligence is fundamentally multi-agent. If you look at how human intelligence came about, it wasn't a single brain sitting alone in a room solving puzzles. It was individuals embedded in groups, cooperating, competing, communicating, developing norms and language and culture. The pressure to model other minds, to coordinate, to deceive and to detect deception, that's plausibly what drove a lot of the growth in our cognitive capabilities in the first place. So if you take that seriously, single-agent learning, which is where most of the field has been, is almost a strange special case.

The second part is more practical. We are now deploying learning systems into the world at scale, and the world is full of other agents, humans and increasingly other AI systems. The moment you have more than one learner in the environment, the environment stops being stationary. Your training signal depends on what the others are doing, and they're adapting to you. That breaks a lot of the assumptions that make standard reinforcement learning work. So we don't really have a choice. If we want these systems to be robust, we have to understand what happens when learning agents interact.

And then there's the part I find most exciting, which is that multi-agent settings give you problems that don't exist in the single-agent world at all. Things like coordination under uncertainty, where you need to reason about what your partner thinks you think. Or the emergence of communication protocols from scratch. Or zero-shot coordination, where you have to work with a partner you've never trained with, which is really the question of how you play well with humans. These are not just harder versions of existing problems. They're qualitatively different, and solving them forces you to confront questions about theory of mind, about conventions, about the structure of common knowledge, that I think are at the core of what intelligence actually is.

So for me it's the frontier because it's where the hard, interesting questions are, and also because it's where the real-world stakes are. Getting cooperation right between learning systems, and between those systems and us, is probably one of the most important things we can work on.

astra-6.text:
I think a lot of what we care about in intelligence only really makes sense in the presence of other agents. Language, for example: you communicate because there’s somebody else who has information you don’t have, or who needs information that you have. Cooperation, negotiation, teaching—these are fundamentally multi-agent activities.

And that changes the learning problem quite profoundly. In a single-agent setting, you can often think of the environment as fixed. But when other agents are learning too, the world changes as you learn. Your actions affect their behaviour, their behaviour affects what you should do, and you may need to reason about what they believe about you. So it’s not just a matter of putting more agents into an existing benchmark. There are new conceptual problems.

One particularly interesting question is whether an agent can cooperate with somebody it hasn’t trained with. Two agents can learn a very effective convention together, but that doesn’t necessarily mean either of them can coordinate with a new partner. If we want AI systems to work with humans, that distinction matters enormously.

So, for me, multi-agent learning is both a route to richer forms of intelligence and a practical necessity. We’re going to have systems interacting with people and with other AI systems. Understanding the behaviour that emerges from those interactions is part of understanding whether the overall system actually does what we want.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a lot of intelligence is fundamentally about interacting with other agents. You’re not just solving a fixed problem in a static environment. You’re dealing with other decision-makers who are learning, adapting, and responding to what you do. Your actions change their behaviour, and their behaviour changes what you ought to do. That makes learning a very different problem.

There’s also this interesting tension between cooperation and competition. Sometimes we have a shared objective, but we still need to work out how to communicate, coordinate, and divide up the task. Sometimes our interests only partially overlap. How do you cooperate in that setting? What can you infer from another agent’s actions, and how should that influence your own?

For me, that’s what makes multi-agent learning such a compelling frontier. If we want AI systems that can work with people and with other AI systems, then social interaction has to be part of what we study. Being very capable in isolation is only part of the picture.
